articles.title: Kraftig fall i nettoinnvandringen til Storbritannia
articles.content:
Med unntak av pandemiårene har nettoinnvandringen til Storbritannia falt til det laveste nivået siden 1997.

– Denne regjeringen har tatt tilbake kontrollen, sier innenriksminister Shabana Mahmood i en kommentar til de nye tallene.

Antallet som flytter til Storbritannia, minus dem som flytter fra landet, utgjør nettoinnvandringen. Den var på 77.000 i tolvmånedersperioden fram til slutten av juni i år, ifølge beregningene til det statistiske sentralbyrået ONS.

Ett år tidligere var tallet 204.000. Siden toppåret 2023, da nettoinnvandringen var på nesten en million mennesker, har nedgangen vært på rundt 90 prosent.

Tallene omfatter ikke migranter som kommer illegalt med småbåter over Den engelske kanal.

Innvandring er et betent politisk tema i Storbritannia, og de nye tallene kan være en fordel for den sittende Labour-regjeringen. Den får hyppig kritikk fra ytre høyre-partiet Reform UK i innvandringsdebatten.

                        A Norwegian minister's response to a question regarding family immigration cases suggests the government are planning to implement a Norwegian language requirement, alongside a review of the income requirement.

During last week's parliamentary session, on November 18th, Progress Party (FrP) MP Erlend Wiborg asked Minister of Justice and Public Security Astri Aas-Hansen: "Will the Minister propose that documented and persistent reluctance to fulfill obligations to learn Norwegian and participate in work or qualification should have consequences for the right to family reunification?"

In response, Aas-Hansen told parliament that Norway’s government was considering introducing a Norwegian language requirement for family immigration cases, alongside a review of the income requirement.

"Good Norwegian language skills are of great importance for the opportunity to become an integrated participant in Norwegian society," she said.

"Good Norwegian language skills are important for being able to contribute, to be able to support oneself, to be able to be an active participant," she added.

"That is why, as I said in my answer to the representative, we are also looking at the possibility of introducing a requirement for Norwegian language skills in cases of family immigration."

The minister also explained that "to ensure more sustainable immigration, better integration and a greater degree of self-sufficiency", the government sees a need to make changes.

These include reviewing the income threshold the person in Norway needs to earn to be able to bring family members to the country, even though the minimum amount was already raised in February 2025.

"People who want family immigration must show that they are financially able to support their family. We are also working on assessing both the size and structure of the maintenance requirement," she said.

When she referred to the ongoing review, the minister was pointing to an earlier decision made by parliament in May this year, where the Storting asked the government to raise the income threshold to at least four times the National Insurance basic amount (at 136,549 kroner in 2026).

Currently, the person living in Norway must prove an annual income of at least 436,957 kroner before tax when applying to bring family members to the country, so if the increase is approved, they would need to earn more than 109,000 kroner extra per year.

However, the hard-right Progress Party's Wiborg was not satisfied with her answer. He said the government had taken too long to consider new measures and called for a clear decision.

"This government has said for five years that it will look at it. It is almost time for the government to come and say what it concludes, not just look at it year after year," he said.

Aas-Hansen replied that the government would not rush its decision.

"Integration is something that must be the responsibility of both the individual and us as a society – that we facilitate it and work to solve the actual challenges we see, to find good solutions and achieve the best possible integration," she said.

"We are taking it at the pace that we believe is right and necessary to actually solve the challenges we face. We will present the case when it is ready to be presented," the minister added.

At this stage, this is only an initial indication of what the government is considering. With immigration and integration under growing pressure, and parties currently negotiating next year's budget and policy priorities, it is natural that these issues are being put on the table.

The minister's comments do not mean that any changes have been officially announced or introduced yet.

As Aas-Hansen made clear, the language requirement is still being reviewed, and there is no concrete news about an income increase either.

Government under pressure as budget deadline hits without an agreement

Norway’s minority Labour government is under growing pressure over the 2027 state budget. The Storting’s Finance Committee has rejected their requests to extend the timetable, so the red-green parties faced a deadline at 10am on Wednesday to present their proposals and changes (the first plan was to decide on it on Friday, November 20th)

This first deadline is just one step in the parliamentary process before the final budget is passed. On Wednesday morning, the parties do not need to present a finished deal, only to clarify their positions. The real test will be when the budget goes to parliament for the final vote on December 7th.

However, just hours before the deadline, the Green Party (MDG) said it will not back up Labour’s latest offer. They warned that Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre must show them a better deal or find another partner for the budget.

"Støre presented a budget with major cuts to climate, nature and public transport, and after these rounds of negotiations, diesel becomes cheaper and emissions increase. Of course, MDG cannot sign an agreement that is so bad for the climate," acting MDG leader Ingrid Liland told newspaper VG.

Without finding common ground and securing a majority to support its proposed budget, there is a risk of a government crisis.

Every autumn, Norwegian health authorities remind people in risk groups to get vaccinated against seasonal viruses like influenza and Covid. This year, though, health organisations are concerned as far fewer older adults in Norway have received the flu vaccine compared to last year.

According to VG, only 38 percent of people over 65 had been vaccinated by November 15th, down from 58 percent at the same time last year. The number os people receiving the Covid-19 vaccination among those over 75 has also dropped, from 39 percent last year to 20 percent so far this season.

This decrease comes as hospital admissions for both flu and Covid-19  also rose last week. So far this year, twice as many people have been hospitalised compared to the same period in 2025.

Magne Wang Fredriksen, Secretary General of the Norwegian Heart, Lung and Stroke Association (LHL), said many people underestimate the risks of influenza.

"This is not just about the elderly who need vaccination. Those who have COPD or other serious illnesses are also at risk of getting sick if those around them are not vaccinated," he said.

Norwegian Food Safety Authority continues efforts to control bird flu outbreak

The Norwegian Food Safety Authority (Mattilsynet) has ordered about 225,000 pullets to be culled at a poultry farm in Rogaland after bird flu was found there in mid-November.

This decision is meant to contain the outbreak and lower the risk of it spreading further.

"Avian influenza is a very serious animal disease, and it can have major consequences if the infection spreads. The regulations therefore have strict requirements for how outbreaks of this disease should be handled," the authority's director general Ingunn Midttun Godal said in a press release.

The farm has responded by filing a formal complaint against the authorities.

"We strongly react to the fact that the culling has been decided without first taking samples from the animals in these houses. We know that animals can be infected without showing signs of illness. But after so many days without signs of illness, it is almost incomprehensible that the decision was made without first examining the animals in more detail," A&A Salte Kyllingoppdrett general manager Andreas Salte wrote in a text message to news agency NTB.

                        Some of Norway's largest cities, such as Bergen and Trondheim, are notorious for wet and grey weather. Therefore, it's no surprise that mould is one of the most common disputes between tenants and landlords.

If you've relocated to Norway from warmer parts of the world, mould might not be among the first things that come to mind when it comes to tenancy disputes.

However, Norway is a country with generally high precipitation levels, especially in its western and central regions.

Mould is often caused by several factors. The first is usually the local weather, but equally important are the overall condition and circumstances of the property (for example, if you're living at the ground floor level, you may experience higher humidity) and how you, as the tenant, use it.

But what should you do if you get a mould problem in your rental home?

Under Norwegian regulations, the initial responsibility for ensuring that there's no mould in a rental property falls on the landlord.

They are responsible for ensuring that the unit has all the essential systems in place to prevent mould from appearing, such as standard ventilation and heating.

You'll also need to invest in a dehumidifier in some buildings.

If you expect your home to have a somewhat high humidity level, the 1,500-6,000 kroner price tag will be well worth it as a mould prevention measure.

That's why many tenants in Bergen in western Norway consider these devices a must-have.

In any case, if you notice mould in your rental home, notify the landlord as soon as possible. If not addressed immediately, it can quickly spread and cause extensive damage.

Are you ensuring a reasonable level of ventilation in your home? Do you let fresh air in and keep the in-built ventilation openings unobstructed and open?

Have you left some space between the furniture and the outer walls? Are you making sure that your home is well-heated?

READ MORE: Landlord or tenant: Who pays which costs in Norway?

If you answered negatively to any of the questions above, you might be at risk of mould in your home.

As the Rent Disputes Tribunal (a state-run entity under the Norwegian Ministry of Local Government) points out on its website, mould thrives on water and temperature, so if you notice high humidity levels in your rental, take action and reduce moisture.

When it comes to maintenance, both the tenant and the landlord have certain rights and obligations.

Unless there's a different agreement or contract in place, the landlord will generally need to take care of maintenance.

You'll still need to look after items and elements that don't fall into the category of fixed property.

Accidental damage repairs don't fall under maintenance – so you'll need to cover these expenses. The same is true if you don't properly care for the property, resulting in mould spreading in the rental.

In many cases, disputes with your landlord regarding mould issues can be resolved through open communication and a clear understanding of both parties' rights and obligations.

Here, addressing concerns swiftly and documenting any communication or actions taken regarding the problem is crucial.

READ MORE: The most common disputes between tenants and landlords

Also, if initial attempts to resolve the dispute fail, you should consider seeking outside assistance - Leieboerforeningen, a national organisation for tenants, and Forbrukerrådet, the Norwegian Consumer Council, can both point you in the right direction.

One avenue for resolving disputes is to submit a complaint to the Rent Disputes Tribunal, which serves as a neutral party to help resolve such disagreements when it comes to rental issues, including mould-related concerns.

You'll need to present your case to the tribunal, which means you'll have to provide evidence and documentation to support your claims.

Extreme cases: Termination of a tenancy contract due to mould

In extreme circumstances, you, as the tenant, have the right to terminate the contract with immediate effect due to mould.

Among other things, the severity of the mould problem and how long the issues have lasted without the landlord rectifying the situation (in cases where such measures fall under their responsibilities).

In any case, the mould issues need to constitute a severe breach of contract if you want to use them as grounds to terminate the lease with immediate effect.

If you're in the right, you will not be obligated to pay rent after leaving the property, and you might also be able to claim compensation for the costs you incurred due to the situation.

However, if you terminate the tenancy agreement without having a right to do so, your landlord may try to claim both rent and compensation for incurred costs and other expenses.

It's always a good idea to consult a legal professional if you're unsure whether this applies to your case.

                        The Norwegian government wants to track immigrant employment and welfare benefit use, no state budget deal yet, KFC arrives in Norway, and more news on Monday.

Norway to track immigrant employment and welfare benefit use

The Norwegian government has asked Statistics Norway (SSB) to create a new yearly employment monitor to track how many immigrants are in the workforce and receiving welfare benefits, according to the newspaper Aftenposten.

"Labour shortages will be one of our major challenges going forward. At the same time, we see that far too many people are on benefits, and we need to get more people to move from benefits to work. This also applies to our immigrant population," Minister of Labour and Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng told news agency NTB.

The government wants to raise overall employment in Norway to 82 percent by 2030 and considers bringing more immigrants into the workforce a crucial part of reaching that goal.

According to SSB figures, the employment rate among immigrants is now 67.5 percent. For refugees, it drops to 54.5 percent, while it is 79.5 percent for the rest of the population.

"The debate about immigration and integration is at times quite polarised. We must not just get hung up on one or the other statistic, but be able to see it as a comprehensive knowledge base and stick to the facts," the minister said.

Stenseng explained the overview will gather data on factors such as immigrant background, how long people have lived in Norway, education, location, and gender. A first version will be released next year, and the full annual overview will begin in 2028.

Aftenposten asked the minister if this could bring more stigmatisation to the immigrant community, to which she replied that she does not think the tracker will have that effect. She argued that clear requirements and targeted support are needed to help more people move from welfare benefits into work.

"I have said that I believe that not making demands is doing people a disservice. Making demands tells people they are needed and ensures they participate. I believe there is no contradiction between making clear demands and at the same time providing the right measures," she added.

Norwegian vocabulary: arbeidsledighet - unemployment​

Friday was the official deadline for the red-green parties, also called the "budget parties", to agree on next year's state budget. But since they did not reach a deal over the weekend, negotiations are continuing on Monday.

During the talks, the main disagreements have been about climate measures and fuel taxes, as well as overall spending and how to pay for higher costs.

The parties trying to reach a deal to be able to secure a majority in parliament  are the Labour Party, the Socialist Left Party (SV), the Green Party (MDG), the Red Party, and the Centre Party (Sp).

Nearly half of Norwegians still oppose EU membership

A new survey from the newspapers Klassekampen and Nationen shows what Norwegians think about joining the European Union.

According to the poll, 31 percent say they would vote yes to EU membership, while 48 percent would vote no. The other 21 percent are undecided.

Norwegian vocabulary: målingen - the poll or the survey

The famous fast-food chain Kentucky Fried Chicken (KFC) is coming to Oslo, opening its first restaurant on Monday, November 23rd in the neighbourhood of Storo.

According to a press release: "Norway is among the first markets in Europe to receive KFC's next-generation restaurant concept, with a renewed visual identity, modern design and a tasty menu with Norwegian touches."

Ronny Gjøse, CEO of KFC Norway, said, "We will combine KFC's flavours with local favourites that our guests already love. Without revealing too much before opening, I can guarantee that there is something for everyone on this menu."

Next week, KFC Oslo City will open its doors, with several more locations planned in Oslo before Christmas. The chain will also start expanding to the rest of the country in the New Year.

Norway has gone viral once again after its Miss Universe contestant made a surprise appearance on Sunday at the 75th edition of the pageant in Puerto Rico. During the national costume parade, the Norwegian representative took to the stage dressed as a troll, paying tribute to Norwegian folklore.

This is not the first time Norway has made headlines with an unusual outfit. In the last edition of the pageant, the country sparked plenty of comments when its representative wore a salmon-inspired costume.

                        With the aim of boosting overall employment in Norway, the government wants to get more immigrants into work. Authorities say they need figures and data to design effective  more targeted measures.

The Norwegian government has asked Statistics Norway (SSB) to create a new yearly employment monitor to track how many immigrants are in the workforce and receiving welfare benefits, according to a press release.

The government wants to raise Norway's employment rate to 82 percent by 2030 and considers bringing more immigrants into the labour market as a key element in achieving that.

According to current figures, the employment rate among immigrants is now 67.5 percent. For refugees, it drops to 54.5 percent, while it is 79.5 percent for the rest of the population.

"Labour shortages will be one of our major challenges going forward. At the same time, we see that far too many people are on benefits, and we need to get more people to move from benefits to work. This also applies to our immigrant population," Minister of Labour and Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng told news agency NTB.

Although Statistics Norway already collects data on employment among the immigrant population, much of this information is published separately. That is why the government wants relevant indicators to be viewed in context and assessed collectively, as explained in the official statement.

Stenseng explained the overview will gather data on factors such as immigrant background, how long people have lived in Norway, education, place of residence and gender. A first version will be out next year and the full annual overview will start in 2028.

"The debate about immigration and integration is at times quite polarised. We must not just get hung up on one or the other statistic, but be able to see it as a comprehensive knowledge base and stick to the facts," the minister said.

Newspaper Aftenposten asked the minister if this could bring more stigmatisation to the immigrant community, to which she replied that she does not think the tracker will have that effect.

"I have said that I believe that not making demands is doing people a disservice. Making demands tells people they are needed and ensures they participate. I believe there is no contradiction between making clear demands and at the same time providing the right measures," she added.

When asked whether the move was a reaction to increasing political pressure on immigration from the right wing, particularly the FrP Progress Party (which is currently the most popular party in Norway), Stenseng denied it. "No. The reason we are doing this, and that I am very concerned about it, is that I believe it is both good and correct social democratic policy to ensure that people are in work. It is one of the most important things for us as individuals."

However, the Progress Party responded quickly on social media, focusing on welfare payments to immigrants. articles.content:

                            Foreigners in Norway earn less than Norwegians and big differences exist between the different immigrant groups.  Pictured is the Oslo opera house.                         Foreigners in Norway typically get paid less than their Norwegian counterparts. However, large differences in earnings also exist among the different immigrant groups.

Immigrants in Norway typically make just over ten percent less than the national average.

The average monthly wage in Norway was 62,070 kroner in 2025. The wage figures from Statistics Norway are pre-tax.

READ MORE: Why Norway's 'average' salary does not reflect reality

Immigrants, on the other hand, earned 55,180 kroner per month, according to figures from the national data agency Statistics Norway.

The gap between foreigners and Norwegians becomes even wider when you compare the wages of immigrants and “other residents” (i.e. non-immigrants). The average salary of other non-immigrant residents is much higher at 64,150 kroner rather than 62,070 per month.

The highest earners among immigrants were those from North America and Oceania. On average, they took home 72,670 kroner each month, considerably more than the national average.

Two other immigrant groups made more than the national average, when measured across all occupations.

Those from the Nordics earned around 67,550 kroner every month. Due to similarities between the languages, it is perhaps easier for them to find work in Norway than for other foreigners.

Meanwhile, those from non-Nordic countries that were part of the EU/EFTA before it expanded in 2004 made 67,100 kroner per month last year, according to the figures.

These immigrant groups likely pulled the average wage for immigrants up overall, as the average dropped significantly after these groups.

Those from Latin America and the Caribbean had an average monthly salary of 57,900 kroner. This was marginally above the average for foreigners.

Foreigners from European countries outside the EU/EFTA, including the UK, earned less than the average at 52,040 kroner.

Foreign residents hailing from Asia could expect to make a comparable amount of money, around 53,220 kroner, every month.

Average wages dropped considerably for the last two immigrant groups. Those hailing from countries which joined the EU after 2004 had typical monthly earnings of 50,810. Meanwhile, Africans had the lowest earnings among all immigrant groups in Norway at 49,530.

READ ALSO: Overqualified and underpaid: The reality facing Norway's foreign workers

Using slightly different figures from Statistics Norway, the study shows that the lowest-earning immigration groups had a higher proportion of workers in the lowest-paying occupations.

For example, just 1,971 foreigners hailing from Africa worked in management, compared to 12,484 in cleaning and helping occupations.

The average wage for somebody in a leadership occupation (across all nationalities) was 108,510 kroner compared to 42,350 kroner per month for a cleaner.

Those immigrants from the Nordics, by contrast, were among the highest-paid workers when measured by the average and median. They also had the highest number of workers in managerial and leadership positions.

There were 5,359 workers in such jobs compared to 1,139 in the lowest wage-earning occupations.

However, this doesn’t fully explain the wage gap. A gap in earnings still exists within the same professions.

When using leadership and managerial roles as an example, those from North America had a monthly paycheck of 98,620 kroner compared to those from countries who only joined the EU after 2004, commanding an average salary of 69,430 kroner.

This lack of parity between different groups was also observed among the lowest wage earners. Foreigners hailing from the Nordics or North America made more money than other foreigners when working in cleaning and help professions.

articles.title: The reasons Norway might reject your Norwegian citizenship application
articles.content:
1 comment
                                                                                            
                                        
                                                                        
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                
                            
                        
                    
                    
                    
                            
                            There are a number of reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) will reject a citizenship application. Photo by Mark König on Unsplash

                        Norwegian citizenship comes with a hefty application fee and plenty of requirements. There are several reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration might reject an application.

Lifetime enrollment in the Norwegian National Insurance Scheme, the ability to live in Norway for as long as you wish, and returning to Norway after a few years away without going through the immigration process are some of the many benefits of Norwegian citizenship.

Norwegian citizenship doesn’t come easy, though. In addition to waiting years to become eligible, you will have to pass language and citizenship tests, provide a criminal record certificate, verify your identity and meet the requirements for permanent residence if you don’t hold it already.

This is all before you pay 6,500 kroner to apply for Norwegian citizenship.

So, what are the reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) turns down applications?

This applies not just to your citizenship application but also to your entire stay. If you bend the rules when it comes to the residence requirements, you could find your citizenship application rejected.

Even if your application is successful, you will find your citizenship revoked later if the UDI finds out. The UDI will still revoke your citizenship, even if you are the one who decides to come clean to them.

Should the authorities have reason to believe that you have provided incorrect information on any residence or citizenship applications, they will typically invite you for an interview with the police or notify you of your revocation in advance.

READ MORE: How Norway can revoke residency and citizenship over wrong details

This one might seem obvious, but it can happen relatively easily. One of the most common reasons for a foreign national having their citizenship rejected is not passing the citizenship or social studies test (in Norwegian).

For the citizenship test, you must answer 24 out of 36 multiple-choice questions correctly.

The social studies test is taken by those who typically have been through the social studies course for immigrants.

Language-wise, you will generally have to have passed an oral test in Norwegian at  B1 level.

Another common pitfall is the criminal record certificate. Criminal record certificates are only valid for three months. The certification proves that you haven’t been convicted of any crimes and are not disqualified from applying for citizenship.

As the certificate can only be valid for three months, the UDI advises that you shouldn’t order the certificate until you have an appointment to hand in your documents to the police. This reduces the likelihood of the certificate expiring before your documents are handed in.

Failure to meet any of the citizenship requirements will result in your application being turned down. You must also hold a valid residence permit whilst applying for citizenship.

Remember that under standard rules, you must have stayed in Norway for a total of eight of the past eleven years and held residence permits that were each valid for at least one year.

On the UDI website, you can learn how to calculate residence periods in exception cases. However, as there is currently a proposal to amend the Citizenship Act, which could alter how qualifying residence time is measured, these requirements may change in the future.

READ MORE: What will Norway's plan to toughen citizenship rules mean for you?

Being convicted of a criminal offence that results in a fine or prison sentence will bar you from being eligible for citizenship for a set period of time.

The disqualification period can range from 2.5 years up to 39 years, depending on the severity of your punishment. You can see an overview of the disqualification rules on the UDI website.

Those who have received fixed penalty notices rather than criminal fines will not be disqualified. Those who have had charges or cases dropped are also not disqualified.

An example of a fixed penalty notice would be a fine for minor or moderate speeding.

To be eligible for citizenship, you also need to be eligible for permanent residence at the same time, which can make matters confusing.

For many, the easiest way around this is to just hold permanent residence as proof of eligibility while applying for citizenship.

The key thing to look out for when it comes to citizenship is the minimum income requirements for non-EEA permanent residence applicants.

One of the requirements for permanent residence applications for non-EEA nationals is that you will need to have fulfilled the income requirements for the previous 12 months and that you cannot have received financial assistance (økonomisk sosialhjelp) during the prior 12 months.

articles.content:
Add a comment
                                                                                            
                                        
                                                                        
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                
                            
                        
                    
                    
                    
                            
                            Norway's Minister of Labour and Inclusion, Kjersti Stenseng, at a Labour Party event in 2023. Photo: Erlend C. L. Birkeland / Arbeiderpartiet / Flickr

                        Immigration and integration have been at the centre of a new row in Norway after a minister was forced to defend and explain her remarks that successive Norwegian governments had been too naive in the past.

Kjersti Stenseng, the Minister of Labour and Inclusion, sparked a row in Norway after stating on public broadcaster NRK's programme Debatten that "we have been too naive" regarding integration, pointing out that too many people are out of work, speak too little Norwegian, and live in areas with challenging living conditions.

Her comments triggered criticism from researcher and sociologist Astrid Ouahyb Sundsbø, who questioned in an opinion piece in NRK whether political rhetoric is part of the problem and if the system created by politicians leads to exclusion.

"If the government is serious about integration, they must stop with the simple rhetoric that immigrants are the problem, and start doing something about the obstacles inherent in the system they themselves have built," Sundsbø wrote, adding: "Placing the problem with refugees and immigrants not only simplifies politics, it also weakens the basis for solutions."

She further wrote that: "Naivety still remains in the understanding of the problem: Immigrants' language, culture and motivation are pointed out, as if the problem lies primarily with 'them' - and the responsibility for solving it too. A less naive understanding would have focused more on the systems we ourselves have built and the obstacles they create."

She even quoted a phrase that many in the international community can identify with: "Even with higher education, many remain stuck at the bottom."

In response, Stenseng explained that when she called Norway’s past approach "too naive," she was talking about politicians, not immigrants.

"When I acknowledge that we have been too naive, it is not a criticism of the people who have come here. We have underestimated how difficult it is to succeed with integration. And here, no party is exempt from criticism," she wrote in a follow-up column for NRK.

Stenseng admitted there have been problems in the past, but said that employment and education among people with immigrant backgrounds have improved over the last ten years.

"Compared to 2015, we see that more people who grow up in homes with parents with an immigrant background attend kindergarten and complete upper secondary education," Stenseng wrote.

"It shows a system that works. But that doesn't exempt us from talking about what doesn't work well enough. And that was also the point of entry into Debatten. It's not a criticism of the people who have come here."

The minister also said: "Integration is about both requirements and opportunities."

Drawing a sharp line against proposals from the right-wing Progress Party (FrP), she argued that slashing Norwegian language training and welfare support will not push newcomers into jobs faster.

"Integration succeeds when we as a society both stand up and make demands. This is also where the important difference between the Labour Party and the Progress Party lies. Some parties apparently believe that lower benefits and less support will solve the integration challenges," she wrote, warning that "demands without opportunities create exclusion."

She ended her column by saying the government will present a new national integration strategy in the spring, which will focus on workforce participation, living conditions, segregation, and cultural barriers that make integration harder.

– Vi fortsetter arbeidet med å komme til enighet med de rødgrønne partiene. Det er helt naturlig at uenighetene i enkelte saker blir tydeligere i denne fasen av forhandlingene....
